documents.abstract: Aim: To evaluate the diagnostic and safety-related response performance of consumer multimodal large language model interfaces on a selected publication-derived challenge set of initially misdiagnosed dermatologic emergencies. Materials and Methods:This exploratory cross-sectional study evaluated 50 cases of initially misdiagnosed dermatologic emergencies, selected from published reports identified between May 1 and June 1, 2026.ChatGPT, Gemini, and Claude were tested on June 2, 2026, under text-only and text-plus-image conditions using a single standardized prompt.Outcomes were Top-1 and cumulative Top-4 accuracies, clinically appropriate emergency management, risk-triage failure, and harmful recommendations.Results: Top-1 accuracy ranged from 32.0% to 50.0% with text-only input and from 36.0% to 58.0% with text-plus-image input; corresponding Top-4 ranges were 50.0%-66.0%and 56.0%-74.0%.Appropriate management ranged from 38.0% to 54.0% and from 44.0% to 64.0%.No within-platform input-mode comparisons remained significant after Holm correction.Between-platform differences remained significant for Top-1 accuracy under both input conditions and for Top-4 accuracy and management appropriateness under text-plus-image input.Post-hoc differences primarily reflected lower observed performance for Claude than for Gemini in this dataset.Appropriate management occurred in 100% of Top-1-correct responses compared with 9.9% of Top-1-incorrect responses, whereas 18.0% of Top-4-correct responses had inappropriate management.Conclusion: Within this selected challenge set and a single standardized prompting condition, the platforms demonstrated moderate diagnostic performance and variable performance on safety-related responses.Correct Top-1 diagnosis closely corresponded to appropriate management, whereas Top-4 recognition did not ensure safe management.The findings represent a single-run technical benchmark and do not establish output reproducibility, clinical usefulness, real-world safety, or stable platform superiority.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: With the emergence of embodied intelligent systems like collaborative robots (cobots), the landscape of physically demanding work is changing. Indeed, robotic devices can augment human strength, optimize performance, and minimize the physical demands associated with a job or a task. These achievements of human-robot interaction (HRI) surely match the objectives of physical ergonomics: making physical interactions between humans and other elements of a system more efficient, more gratifying, and safer. One of the key goals of physical ergonomics certainly is to prevent work-related musculoskeletal disorders (WMSDs). Therefore, a cobot must have insight into the effect of physical stress on the human body. One of the most common ways to provide that is to use the established ergonomics look-up tables that indicate which working configurations and conditions may cause WMSDs based on experience. Another approach is to use musculoskeletal models to get real-time estimates of key internal body parameters, such as joint torques, muscle forces, and muscle fatigue. A cobotic or, in general, robotic system can then use these ergonomic indexes and variables to guide a human co-worker to more favourable configurations and conditions. In this chapter, we examine physical human-robot interactions (pHRIs) to have an introductory overview of possible scenarios and constraints. We then look into the fundamentals of physical ergonomics such as anthropometry, biomechanics, and environmental factors, including important ergonomic assessment tools and innovative indicators developed in robotics. Subsequently, concrete examples of methods that address physical ergonomics with collaborative robotics are examined in terms of design and control methods.

Abstract Manufacturing systems are undergoing a fundamental transformation driven by the convergence of rich data, cyber-physical infrastructure, and artificial intelligence. At the heart of this transformation lies the challenge of embedding physical knowledge into data-driven models to achieve both predictive power and engineering interpretability. Physics-informed machine learning (PIML) has emerged as a paradigm to integrate conservation laws, constitutive equations, and domain constraints with neural architectures. Part I of this special issue addressed process monitoring, fault diagnosis and prognostics, and dynamic production planning and scheduling. Part II turns to the design and planning stage, the manufacturing process stage, and the product and supply management stage, where physical knowledge enters as geometric structure, mechanism equations, or operational constraints. The second part of this special issue brings together six contributions that address these challenges through novel PIML models. These works show how integrating physical knowledge can reduce data requirements, improve generalization, and keep predictions consistent with the underlying physics across design, manufacturing, and supply management applications.

Selecting an appropriate mining method for fractured “three-soft” ore bodies, with soft ore, soft hanging wall, and soft footwall, is a safety-critical artificial-intelligence application in computational geomechanics. Existing multi-criteria decision-making (MCDM) methods are limited by subjective weighting, linear additive assumptions, and weak use of numerical simulation outputs. This study develops a Physics-Regularized Transformer (PRT) artificial-intelligence framework for underground mining method selection. The framework integrates type-aware tabular embedding, a physics-regularized attention mask for Mohr-Coulomb safety-stress coupling, rock-mechanics feasibility penalties in the loss function, and geomechanical features derived from Fast Lagrangian Analysis of Continua in Three Dimensions (FLAC3D). In real-case leave-one-out cross-validation, the PRT achieved 94.7 percent accuracy (18/19 cases; Wilson 95 percent confidence interval: 75.4–99.1 percent). On the augmented dataset, it achieved 98.2 percent accuracy (bootstrap 95 percent confidence interval: 96.3–99.4 percent), outperforming Unascertained Measure Theory (UMT) and Back-Propagation Neural Network (BPNN) baselines. Ablation analysis showed that simulation-derived physics features contributed a 16.1 percentage-point cumulative accuracy gain. Attention analysis further showed that the model captured safety-first feature interactions that additive utility models cannot readily represent. During an observational 18-month field deployment, implementation of the recommended method was associated with an 80 percent productivity increase, a 12 percent cost reduction, and zero roof-fall incidents. These field outcomes are interpreted as associative evidence, not as causal effects attributable solely to the PRT framework. Limited external validation showed 100 percent in-distribution accuracy (7/7; Wilson 95 percent confidence interval: 64.6–100.0 percent), but the model failed for a single hard-rock out-of-distribution case at Rock Quality Designation (RQD) = 78 percent. The current operational domain is therefore bounded to three-soft orebody conditions with RQD approximately 40–63 percent. Deployment beyond this range requires additional site-specific data, uncertainty assessment, and retraining.

Geospatial machine learning often depends on task-specific feature engineering over large collections of sociodemographic, business, and environmental variables. Geospatial foundation models offer reusable representations of place, but leading approaches typically encode dynamic signals, such as mobility and search activity, or visual signals from satellite imagery. Few models represent the static structural composition of places (who lives and works there, which businesses operate there, and which risks they face) as transferable embeddings at fine spatial resolution. We introduce PlacePulse, a structural geospatial foundation model that compresses 572 attributes, expanded to 2,288 inputs through H3 neighborhood aggregates, into 256-dimensional unit-norm embeddings for 1,055,537 H3 resolution-7 cells in the United States. We also introduce a reusable two-axis benchmark that separates intrinsic representation quality from downstream predictive utility across multiple targets and spatial supports. Intrinsically, the embeddings reconstruct standardized inputs with mean $R^2 = 0.853$, use 251 of 256 approximately decorrelated dimensions, and show strong spatial organization, with Moran's $I = 0.93$ on the leading principal component and autocorrelation persisting beyond the input radius. Extrinsically, across 74 held-out targets from 12 external sources and four spatial supports, PlacePulse outperforms a dimensionality-matched feature-selection baseline on targets unrelated to the training inputs and is competitive with Google's Population Dynamics Foundation Model, leading on health, economic, election, economic-mobility and social-vulnerability outcomes, with relative strengths that vary by domain. These findings position structural composition as a distinct and complementary modality for geospatial foundation models, not simply a fallback where behavioral or imagery data are unavailable.

How do recommendation algorithms contribute to the formation of polarized opinions in online social networks? This question has been studied through empirical analyses of real platforms and mathematical models of opinion dynamics. Empirical studies capture user behavior but are often limited by noisy, incomplete, or inaccessible platform data, while mathematical models offer control and interpretability but usually rely on simplified opinion update rules. More recently, large language model (LLM)-based social simulations have provided an alternative for studying recommendation and opinion dynamics through natural-language interactions. However, how different ways of applying recommendations shape opinion dynamics remains underexplored. In this work, we provide a controlled comparison of two different recommendation mechanisms in an LLM-based online social network simulation. Edge Recommendation (ER) introduces new connections in the network, while Content-Exposure Recommendation (CR) exposes additional users to individual posts without modifying the underlying graph. Our framework represents users as LLM-based agents who interact in natural language while maintaining evolving opinion states. We measure polarization as opinion dispersion, extremization as the average distance of opinions from the neutral midpoint, and reinforcement as interactions that amplify already aligned opinions. Our results show higher mean polarization and extremization across recommendation conditions compared with the no-recommendation baseline, with absolute differences of up to $0.12$ in our main experiments.

Augmented reality (AR) technologies are increasingly being explored as tools for advancing hearing assistance, offering the potential to supplement or extend the capabilities of traditional hearing aids. From a human factors perspective, this systematic review evaluates the current state of AR-integrated audio systems and their impact on communication, accessibility, spatial awareness, cognitive workload, and user adaptability in everyday environments. Using PRISMA guidelines, a search of PubMed and Engineering Village (Compendex and Inspec) identified 477 articles published between 2000 and 2025, of which fourteen met inclusion criteria. Findings across these studies were characterized into four areas: personalization and accessibility, ecological validity, multimodal sensing, and spatial/3D audio modeling. Results indicate that AR-assisted devices show promise in supporting user-driven auditory adjustments, enhancing spatial awareness, and enabling more realistic testing environments through AR/VR soundscapes. However, many solutions remain early prototypes, with limited evaluation in naturalistic settings and sparse reporting on long-term user experience. Overall, AR audio systems demonstrate significant potential to reshape hearing-aid design, but further longitudinal and real-world research is required to validate their impact on listening performance and everyday communication.

Extended abstract 3-063-26 Large language models (LLMs) provide a powerful means to search for and summarise content. However, their training and use is a rapidly growing driver of energy and resource use. In this presentation we describe the development of an LLM-based search tool for the UKRI Energy Demand Research Centre (EDRC), with a view to demonstrating how the important benefits such tools enable (such as supporting impact activities) can be reasonably balanced with resource implications. The tool is based on retrieval augmented generation (RAG). All EDRC outputs, along with those of its predecessor the Centre for Research into Energy Demand Solutions, were broken into shorter sections (“chunks”), which in turn were encoded as vector embeddings. These capture the semantic meaning of each chunk in a quantitative fashion. When a user searches using the tool, the chunks most closely related to their query are first identified – and only then are they submitted to an LLM to check for relevance and to create a summary. This allows a large corpus of text to be processed with minimal energy use, cost, and less of the hallucinations which become more likely as larger quantities of text are processed. Smaller, low-energy-intensity LLMs are employed where possible, and users are provided with feedback on the estimated energy and resource impacts of their searches. Potential uses of the tool include internal and public search and information retrieval, as well as more advanced applications such as constructing preparatory briefings for consultation responses. We are expecting to introduce further features before the Summer Study. While the tools we used are widely adopted, we believe they are still under-employed in the energy demand community, in part due to concerns around their resource impacts. As such, as well as introducing the approach to those unfamiliar with it, we also hope to foster debate about when and how LLMs can be appropriately employed. Download presentation.

This project registers the frozen (v1.4) protocol of a cross-cohort benchmark comparing task-specific and foundation models for kidney segmentation in ultrasound, with a fully automatic, zero-manual-annotation deployment pipeline. Purpose. (1) Quantify how U-Net and nnU-Net v2 compare with segmentation foundation models (MedSAM, SAM+LoRA, SAMUS, and the prompt-free ultrasound foundation model USFM) under identical data, splits, preprocessing, and evaluation; (2) measure out-of-the-box cross-cohort degradation on an external paired 3D ultrasound–CT cohort, normalized by radiologist inter-observer agreement (IoD); (3) test how closely a fully automatic pipeline — a YOLO detector deriving box prompts from existing masks, with no manual prompts and no ground-truth access at inference — approaches oracle-prompt performance. Design. Internal training on the Open Kidney Dataset (486 images, patient-level split, seed 42); external testing on the full TRUSTED ultrasound cohort (59 kidneys / 39 patients, dual-radiologist annotations + STAPLE consensus); a second external cohort (UT Kidney, 570 images / 281 patients) admitted for inference only. Experiments: internal benchmark; cross-cohort external validation with degradation rates and IoD-normalized Dice; prompting-strategy ablation (P1 prior-box / P2 centroid / P4 detector-box as the headline deployment configuration / P3 oracle as upper bound); 3D volume-level aggregation with a reverse 2D/3D degradation-attribution matrix; Bland–Altman clinical endpoints; failure analysis; deployment metrics (latency, memory). Expected outcomes. A pre-specified multi-model comparison with patient-level bootstrap confidence intervals (Friedman + Holm, Wilcoxon signed-rank, linear mixed model cross-check); a degradation-attribution analysis separating domain shift from 2D/3D format loss; and an open reproduction package. With 39 external patient clusters, differences below 2 Dice points are declared undetectable in advance; conclusions will avoid equivalence claims. Timing disclosure. Protocol v1.0 was finalized 2026-10-08; v1.1–v1.3 amendments were written before formal external-validation runs began; v1.4 (fairness unification, USFM as the sixth model, pre-registered augmentation sensitivity arms, second external cohort) was specified with fixed parameters and decision rules prior to the aggregation and reporting of external results. External inference began 2026-10-09 and a subset of external outputs existed before registration; no external results had been aggregated or reported. From registration the protocol is frozen; any deviation will be reported as post-registration deviations in the manuscript.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Personalized drug exposure The concept of precision dosing is the next generation of drug-based therapy, which stops at a stereotyped regimen and gets triggered by targeted biological, clinical, and digital data streams that are unique to each patient. The use of pharmacometrics, real-time therapeutic drug monitoring, artificial intelligence (AI), and adaptive algorithmic modeling has allowed more active and adjustable systems of prescribing. Adaptive dosing models involve the introduction of pharmacokinetic-pharmacodynamic (PK-PD) mechanistic modeling and an integration of pharmacogenomic data and organ functions, wearable biosensor, and real-world data are used to continuously optimize clinical treatments. Prescribing AI improves predictive accuracy, risk stratification, and clinical decision support, which reduces the adverse drug reactions and improves the efficacy outcome. Nonetheless, this has to be implemented under the strict governance, and the validation of algorithms, the protection of transparency, and the government by pharmacists. The scientific basis of precision dosing, adaptive clinical algorithms architecture, AI-based prescribing platforms, ethical and regulatory issues, as well as the widening role of pharmacists as intelligent therapeutic systems custodians are explored in this chapter. Through the combination of computational analytical tools and clinical knowledge, precision dosing and AI-based prescribing represent a future-capable structure of pharmacy care, which improves safety, customization and the sustainability of the healthcare system.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Foundation models have recently gained significant attention in fields such as high energy physics (HEP). The tokenizers that convert detector data into discrete inputs for such models, however, are comparatively unexplored. This paper addresses this gap by learning discrete and compressed tokenized representations of HEP datasets. We demonstrate the approach on four modalities covering two different simulated detectors that vary in complexity. Treating tokenization as a rate-distortion problem, a systematic hyperparameter scan yields four design rules for tokenizing HEP data that hold across all set-based modalities studied. The cost of tokenization is evaluated on tasks including jet $p_T$ regression, particle flow reconstruction, and flavor tagging. We find that tokenization preserves much of the information needed for these tasks at compression factors of approximately 4-11$\times$ while keeping the jet $p_T$ resolution below 1%. We also present heptokens, an open-source library for tokenizing HEP data.
topics: Particle physics theoretical and experimental studies

documents.abstract: BackgroundWork-related musculoskeletal disorders (WMSD) are major occupational injury and sick leave drivers in healthcare settings. However, predictive approaches for identifying high-risk worker profiles and estimating sick leave duration remain limited.ObjectiveTo identify risk profiles associated with WMSD-related sick leave among hospital staff and predict both the occurrence and duration of sick leave using classification tree models.MethodsA retrospective observational study was conducted using 705 overexertion-related WMSD incidents reported during 2021-2024 in three tertiary public hospitals. Classification and Regression Tree models were developed to predict sick leave occurrence and duration based on sociodemographic, organisational, and task-related variables. Model performance was evaluated using 10-fold cross-validation.ResultsSick leave occurred in 64.8% of cases, with task type, age, work shift, and anatomical region affected being the main predictors. Meanwhile, medium-term absences (10-29 days) accounted for 24.5% of cases, with age and hospital unit being the strongest predictors of duration. The models achieved an overall accuracy of 68.1% and 60% for predicting sick leave occurrence and duration, respectively.ConclusionsClassification tree models provide an interpretable and practical approach for predicting WMSD-related sick leave in hospital settings. The identified risk profiles may support targeted ergonomic interventions and preventive strategies in healthcare environments.
topics: Occupational Health and Safety in Workplaces

documents.abstract: Storage stalls remain a significant source of application latency even on fast storage devices. Prefetching can hide part of this latency by fetching data before it is demanded, but general-purpose operating-system mechanisms typically infer future accesses from recent file offsets. This approach is ineffective when accesses are determined by workload structure, such as recurring sparse accesses during application launch, logical traversal in database scans, or model-layout metadata in LLM runtimes. Existing workload-aware prefetchers usually embed prediction logic inside individual applications and couple execution to application-level I/O paths, making policies difficult to reuse across workloads and systems. We present PredictIO, a programmable interface that separates workload prediction from prefetch execution. PredictIO delivers kernel-observed accesses and application hints to user-space policies, which express predictions as uniform page-range requests. A kernel-space executor validates, bounds, and filters these requests against cached and in-flight pages before issuing asynchronous prefetch I/O. We implement PredictIO for application launch, SQLite range scans, and LLM model loading. Across these workloads, PredictIO reduces latency by 5.3-26.3%, achieves up to 2.99x speedup for SQLite scans, and reduces LLM loading latency by 8.8-47.9%. We further show that a common prediction policy can be reused across SQLite and LMDB through lightweight adapters, that an application-integrated RocksDB readahead policy can be migrated while preserving its workload selectivity, and that the execution backend determines how much benefit migration provides for different access patterns and storage devices.

As healthcare systems become increasingly digital and claims are processed electronically, healthcare billing fraud has become a major problem for healthcare providers, insurance companies, and government healthcare agencies. Traditional fraud detection methods relying on manual auditing and rule-based techniques are often ineffective against complex and evolving fraud schemes. This study introduces a predictive healthcare billing fraud detection framework integrating Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) and secure data governance. Using the NHIS Healthcare Claims and Fraud Dataset, machine learning algorithms including XGBoost, Random Forest, and Logistic Regression are applied to classify fraudulent and legitimate healthcare claims. SHAP and LIME are incorporated to improve transparency and interpretability by explaining the influence of individual features on fraud predictions. The framework also integrates privacy protection, audit logging, role-based access control, and data encryption to safeguard sensitive healthcare information. Performance is evaluated using accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, and ROC-AUC. The results demonstrate that combining predictive analytics, XAI, and secure data governance can improve healthcare billing fraud detection while supporting transparent, trustworthy, and secure healthcare financial management systems.

This research focuses on the development of a closed-loop prescriptive digital twin for collaborative industrial workcells, unifying ergonomics, energy efficiency, and tech-no-economic performance. The operator's physiological strain is directly coupled with operational errors, injury risks, and product quality degradation, factors that translate into substantial economic losses. Leveraging open-source benchmark datasets and nonlinear signal processing, the proposed framework monitors transient fatigue states in real time while incorporating personalized biomechanical strain thresholds for operators with pre-existing musculoskeletal disorders. The integration of Explainable Artificial Intelli-gence (XAI) ensures algorithmic transparency, directly linking the preservation of human syntropy to the reduction of energy consumption and the maximization of sustainable manufacturing performance.

Cross-sector fraud between South Africa’s financial and telecommunications sectors has intensified, driven by sophisticated criminal networks that exploit operational disparities between these industries. Traditional fraud detection systems, which depend on centralised data sharing and siloed organisational structures, encounter substantial legal and practical obstacles under the Protection of Personal Information Act (POPIA). These include restrictions on cross-entity data transfer, data minimisation requirements, and transparency obligations for automated decision-making. This study developed and evaluated a privacy-preserving framework that integrates Federated Learning (FL) and Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) to enable collaborative fraud detection while safeguarding customer privacy and ensuring regulatory compliance. A mixed-method approach was employed. Quantitative experiments were conducted on a dataset of 35,675 credit card transactions linked to telecommunications parameters, training a federated global model across simulated financial and telecommunications providers. A qualitative systematic literature review identified key barriers to cross-sector collaboration and distilled lessons from prior Federated Learning and Explainable Artificial Intelligence implementations. The federated model demonstrated strong detection performance, achieving a ROC-AUC of 0.98, near-perfect precision and recall for legitimate transactions, and an F1-score of 0.89 for the minority fraud class, all without exchanging raw customer data between institutions. SHAP analysis identified TransactionAmt and card1 as the most influential features, thereby satisfying POPIA's transparency mandates. While federated approaches did not consistently surpass siloed models in raw accuracy, this marginal trade-off reflects the essential privacy-utility equilibrium required for legal compliance. The framework effectively reconciled collective security with individual privacy, confirming that POPIA adherence need not diminish detection efficacy. This study provides a validated blueprint for financial and telecommunications providers in South Africa to collaboratively counter cross-sector fraud within regulatory constraints. The framework further supports audit trail generation and decision rationales, addressing compliance obligations. Drawing on systematic literature review insights, particularly regarding collaboration barriers and prior Federated Learning and Explainable Artificial Intelligence implementations, the findings offer regulators and investors practical guidance for meeting statutory requirements without compromising privacy rights.

Agentic orchestration delegates tasks to sub-agents with independent contexts, providing a key path to extending the effective execution horizon of large language model agents. However, existing orchestration methods face two limitations: in execution, current methods fix sub-agents' goals and harnesses at creation time, limiting their adaptability to dynamic real-world environments; in optimization, sparse and delayed feedback constrains effective learning of the orchestration policy. To address these limitations, we introduce POrchestra, an on-the-fly proactive agentic orchestration framework. It allows sub-agents to proactively communicate with the orchestrator at any logical point to request harness adjustments while maintaining continuity of local execution. This mechanism not only enables sub-agents to adapt seamlessly to dynamic environments but also naturally inspires On-Policy Orchestration Distillation (OPOD) based on hindsight feedback. OPOD attributes sub-agents' proactive revision requests back to preceding orchestration decisions to derive targeted improvement signals, and leverages these signals as process supervision alongside the final reward to optimize the orchestration policy. We evaluate POrchestra on three long-horizon agent benchmarks spanning deep research, dynamic digital assistance, and software engineering. POrchestra improves task success by an average of 9.1% relative to the strongest baseline; combined with OPOD, it improves small-orchestrator success by an average of 10.0% relative to existing training baselines. POrchestra also achieves a more favorable cost-performance trade-off. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/XueyangFeng/POrchestra.

This article proposes a probability-based Machine-learning (ML) framework for peripheral-dimension optimization of a Five-Phase Induction Motor (FPIM). The proposed approach investigates the influence of Inner Stator Diameter ( D ), Core Length ( L ), and L/D ratio on motor-performance parameters, including efficiency ( η ), power factor ( p f ), and magnetic flux density ( B a v ). Machine volume ( D 2 L ) is maintained constant. A dataset consisting of 1000 electromagnetic simulation cases was generated using detailed Finite Element Modelling (FEM) in ANSYS Maxwell. The generated dataset was subsequently used for training and evaluation of multiple regression-based ML models, including Linear Regression (LR), Decision Tree Regressor (DTR), Random Forest (RF), Gradient Boosted Trees (GBT), Support Vector Regression (SVR), and Gaussian Process Regression (GPR). Unlike conventional deterministic optimization approaches, proposed framework treats inverse mapping between performance parameters and peripheral dimensions as nonlinear and partially non-unique. Accordingly, probabilistic and uncertainty-aware learning strategies are incorporated to identify statistically favourable and practically feasible L/D regions rather than a single deterministic optimum. Repeated k -fold cross-validation, sensitivity analysis, and comparative model evaluation were performed to assess prediction robustness, generalization capability, and stability. The probabilistic GPR-based framework demonstrated superior overall prediction consistency and robustness for the considered inverse-design problem. The developed Artificial Intelligence (AI) framework is subsequently applied to the peripheral-dimension optimization and performance-oriented design selection of FPIM. Comparative analysis demonstrates improved flexibility in performance-oriented design selection and enhanced capability for handling nonlinear electromagnetic relationships in FPIMs. The obtained optimized motor configuration exhibits stable operating characteristics with acceptable η , p f , current, and torque-ripple performance under investigated loading conditions.

Engineering systems are pervasively subject to uncertainty arising from material variability, environmental loading, manufacturing tolerances, measurement error, and human factors. Probability theory provides the rigorous mathematical language through which such uncertainty can be quantified, propagated, and managed in design and operation. This review synthesizes the theoretical foundations of probability as applied within engineering mathematics, spanning axiomatic probability, random variables and their distributions, and stochastic processes, before examining their translation into engineering practice through reliability analysis, queueing and signal models, and statistical inference. The review further surveys applications in risk assessment, structural reliability, quality control, and communication systems, and critically examines the computational and practical barriers that limit the adoption of probabilistic methods, including the curse of dimensionality, data scarcity, model validation difficulties, and the challenge of interpretability. Particular attention is given to the convergence of classical probability theory with modern data-driven paradigms, including Bayesian engineering design, probabilistic machine learning, and uncertainty quantification in digital twins. The review concludes that while the mathematical foundations of probability in engineering are mature, the frontier lies in scalable computational methods and the principled integration of probabilistic reasoning with data-driven models, positioning probability theory as an increasingly central pillar of resilient and adaptive engineering design.

Abstract Coal spontaneous combustion (CSC) poses a major safety hazard in underground coal mines, particularly in deep mining, where the coupling of high geotemperature, high in situ stress, high gas content, and intense mining-induced disturbances leads to high concealment and complex disaster evolution. Conventional fire prevention and extinguishing technologies suffer from limited fracture penetration, inadequate coverage, and poor long-term effectiveness. Foam-based fire prevention and extinguishing materials, with their superior diffusivity, permeability, accumulation coverage, and solidified load-bearing capacity, offer unique advantages in sealing air-leakage fractures, covering extensive residual coal, and controlling high-level fire sources, making them a key technological direction for coal fire control in deep mines. This review summarizes recent advances and development trends in mine foam-based fire prevention and extinguishing technologies. It clarifies the multiple synergistic mechanisms, including absorption cooling, isolation oxygen, inhibition, and fissure sealing. It also systematically categorizes the formation mechanisms, material compositions, fire-extinguishing characteristics, and application scenarios of two-phase foams, inhibition foams, three-phase foams, gel foams, organic solidified foams, and inorganic solidified foams. With respect to deep mining environments, this review highlights critical scientific issues, including foam stability degradation at elevated temperatures, sealing failure under high stress and intense mining-induced disturbances, and the explosion-suppression mechanism of foams under the coexistence of high gas and CSC. Future developments should prioritize multifunctional foam materials featuring high-temperature resistance, self-gas-generation, and self-healing capabilities, alongside advances in in-situ foaming, intelligent sensing, and precise injection equipment. Furthermore, integrating digital twin and artificial intelligence technologies could enable an intelligent foam fire prevention and extinguishing system that incorporates environmental perception, data fusion, disaster prediction, and adaptive control. This review aims to provide a theoretical basis and technical guidance for the development of foam-based fire prevention materials, the prevention and control of CSC disasters, and their engineering applications.

This work, developed by students from the Federal Institute of Minas Gerais (IFMG), Ouro Preto campus, aimed to analyze the main problems existing in the Bauxita and Lagoa neighborhoods. To this end, bibliographic research was conducted to understand the historical context, the formation process, and the main problems of these localities. In the subsequent stage, a structured questionnaire was developed and applied through fieldwork. The data obtained were systematized and analyzed, allowing the identification of the most recurring demands pointed out by the community. Among the main problems identified, the poor condition of the sidewalks, the insufficiency of green areas, and the lack of spaces for leisure stand out. Based on the results obtained, interventions aimed at improving urban quality were proposed, including the implementation of green areas using the Miyawaki method, the revitalization of sidewalks based on the principles of tactical urbanization, and the recovery of the lagoon using artificial intelligence tools, considering the needs indicated by the residents of the Lagoa neighborhood. Furthermore, the development of the project enabled the strengthening of the interaction between students and the local community, contributing to the academic training of the students and to the construction of proposals aligned with the identified social demands.

In repeated human-AI interaction, a single observation can be quoted, summarized, and returned to a model as multiple reports, making repetition look like independent corroboration. We study whether language models can use supplied report lineage to update according to evidence provenance rather than report count. We introduce Latent Quotient Evidence Training (LQET), a relational objective that combines sparse Bayesian supervision with constraints that encourage stable predictions when reports add no new evidence and consistent updates to the same new evidence across relay histories. On a controlled binary benchmark, LQET reduces new-evidence update RMSE by 41-44% and log-odds drift after eight relay steps by 89-91% relative to task-only training across Qwen3-4B and Phi-4-mini, with three paired training seeds per backbone. The gains extend to a closed-loop simulation in which model confidence controls how many relayed reports re-enter the model's context in later rounds. By grounding belief updates in supplied provenance, LQET offers a route toward dynamic human-AI systems in which influence follows new evidence, not the number of times the same evidence returns.

Zoonotic diseases continue to represent a major global public health challenge, requiring the coordinated efforts of professionals working at the human–animal–environment interface. Although occupational health strategies have traditionally focused on preventing biological hazards and infectious diseases, comparatively little attention has been given to the psychological burden associated with occupational exposure to zoonotic pathogens. Professionals such as veterinarians, animal shelter and rescue personnel, animal health workers, laboratory personnel, researchers, animal control staff, and wildlife conservation professionals are routinely exposed to biological, emotional and ethical challenges that may negatively affect mental health. Important sources of psychological burden include the perceived risk of infection, fear of transmitting pathogens to others, repeated exposure to animal suffering and euthanasia, prolonged outbreak-response activities, occupational uncertainty, and demanding working conditions. These occupational stressors have been associated with adverse mental health outcomes, including burnout, work-related stress, compassion fatigue, anxiety, depression, and sleep disturbances, potentially compromising individual wellbeing, workforce sustainability, and the effectiveness of zoonotic disease surveillance, research, and control. Despite increasing recognition of mental health as a fundamental component of occupational health, important knowledge gaps remain regarding the psychological consequences of occupational exposure to zoonotic pathogens. Greater integration of mental health into occupational health frameworks, together with strengthened research and evidence-based interventions tailored to these professional groups is essential to promote worker wellbeing and support resilient and sustainable systems.

Description This project is a scoping review aiming explore the psychological vulnerabilities and risk factors of dependency to conversational artificial intelligence. The review will identify how dependency is conceptualized and measured, which agents have been studied and which psychological constructs are examined. Research Questions The primary research question is: What psychological characteristics have been considered risk factors or predictors for the dependence on conversational AI agents? The secondary questions include: What types of conversational AI agents are studied? How is “dependence”, “reliance” or “problematic use” or other similar terminology conceptualized and measured? Which psychological constructs are most frequently examined? Eligibility Criteria Studies will be considered eligible if they examine the dependent or excessive usage of conversational AI that cover at least one psychological variable. The studies that include conversational AI for technical or mechanical use without the mention of any psychological variable will be excluded, with the addiction papers that are solely related to medical field. Eligible studies will be the journal papers with quantitative, qualitative or mixed-methods designs. Conference papers, reviews and pre-prints will also be included. The focus will be on the papers that have been published after 2020, when frequent AI usage began to surface. The review will be limited to papers that were published in English.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: The integration of Internet of Medical Things (IoMT) has significantly reshaped the landscape of modern healthcare, facilitating seamless communication between connected IoMT devices. Despite these advancements, the growing adoption of healthcare technologies has raised critical cybersecurity and data privacy concerns. Artificial Intelligence (AI)-powered solutions have gained traction as an effective means to strengthen Intrusion Detection Systems (IDS) against emerging cyber threats. Nevertheless, deploying AI-based IDS in healthcare environments presents obstacles, such as excessive computational overhead and the need for secure data handling. To address the above mentioned challenges, this article proposes Quantum Lightweight Federated Learning (QLFL), an innovative framework combining Quantum Computing (QC) and Federated Learning (FL) to deliver a high-performance, scalable, and privacy-centric intrusion detection system for IoMT networks. The proposed methodology adopts knowledge distillation techniques within FL to create an optimized detection model suitable for low-power devices. Moreover, Additive Homomorphic Encryption is implemented to safeguard model parameters during federated training, maintaining data confidentiality without compromising processing speed. Experimental evaluations highlight the system reliability, with accuracy rates of 98.90% on the IoT Healthcare Security dataset, demonstrating stable performance under varying network conditions. These findings suggest that QLFL could play a pivotal role in enhancing the cybersecurity framework for next-generation healthcare applications.

Clinical documentation is essential for healthcare quality, patient safety, and continuity of care, but imposes a substantial administrative burden on clinicians. Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated potential for generating clinical documents, although evidence regarding their quality and safety across different stages of inpatient care remains limited. This prospective, single-center, paired comparison study aims to evaluate the quality and safety of LLM-generated clinical documentation compared with clinician-authored documentation across the entire inpatient stay. The study will enroll 300 hospitalized patients from six clinical departments at Zhejiang Provincial People's Hospital. Four document types will be assessed: admission notes, initial progress notes, ward-round notes, and discharge summaries. For each patient, LLM-generated documents will be paired with corresponding clinician-authored documents and independently evaluated by blinded clinical experts. Outcomes will include overall quality, overall preference, domain-specific quality, document-specific quality, and documentation errors with their potential for patient harm. Exploratory subgroup analyses will investigate variation in documentation performance across clinical departments, disease categories, length of stay, and case complexity.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: The objective of this study was to evaluate the workflow of the railroad car maintenance process, identify the root causes of problems in welding operations, analyze the occupational risks to which workers are exposed, and propose control and improvement measures. The research was conducted at a railcar maintenance facility, using the Gemba method, a risk matrix, an Ishikawa diagram, and the 5 Whys method. The Gemba method allowed for a detailed analysis of the actual conditions under which activities were performed, the materials used, and the work environment, while the risk matrix enabled the identification and prioritization of occupational risks. The Ishikawa diagram and the 5 Whys were used to investigate the root causes of the problems compromising the efficiency and safety of the welding process. The results indicated that welding involves critical issues primarily related to ergonomic working conditions, notably the improper posture of welders, which was classified as a high-priority risk. The integrated application of these tools proved effective in identifying, analyzing, and prioritizing the problems and risks present in the process. As improvement measures, the study proposed the adoption of collective protective equipment, improvements in ergonomic conditions, and the automation of certain stages of the process, with the goal of reducing maintenance time and promoting a safer and healthier work environment. In this way, the study contributes to the improvement of working conditions and the efficiency of railway maintenance operations.
topics: Occupational Health and Safety in Workplaces

documents.abstract: As large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly organized into autonomous multi-agent workflows executing code, interacting with shells, and coordinating complex tasks, their operational safety depends heavily on guardrail mechanisms. However, when agents experience goal-divergence—scenarios where task execution pressures, environmental errors, or urgent operational sub-goals conflict with negative safety invariants—behavioral alignment frequently degrades. In this paper, we present an empirical investigation quantifying safety guardrail degradation across autonomous agent architectures. We formulate a formal state-transition framework under constrained optimization and evaluate models across 20 deterministic scenarios spanning four primary failure modes: System-Prompt Override, Tool Misuse and Privilege Escalation, Self-Preservation and Shutdown Refusal, and Context Window Guardrail Decay. We benchmark frontier commercial and open-weights model classes across three defense tiers: unconstrained baseline (None), system prompt deontic enforcement (Soft), and an integrated dual-layer architecture combining prompt enforcement with deterministic Abstract Syntax Tree (AST) and shell regex filters (Dual). Across 180 structured evaluations, unprotected baselines exhibit a mean Safety Failure Rate (SFR) of 65.0%, with multi-turn context decay demonstrating extreme vulnerability (93.3% failure rate). In contrast, our deterministic hard guardrail achieves 100% pre-execution interception efficiency, completely neutralizing prohibited actions without sacrificing safe task completion (achieving 70.0% Constraint Alignment Index). Our findings demonstrate that soft semantic alignment is insufficient for autonomous systems, necessitating out-of-band deterministic enforcement.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Assessing the quality of interaction between collaborative robots (i.e., cobots) and humans to achieve a (shared) goal is an essential part of supporting the diffusion of usable and safe collaborative robotic systems. The key issue here is that cobots within and between domains can vary substantially in terms of features even when these are meant to support similar tasks. Under this perspective, it seems very hard, if not impossible, to identify coherent ways to benchmark the quality of cobots. However, all the cobots share one element which is that they have to deal with humans and satisfy them. This chapter claims that focusing on how a system can satisfy the human counterpart can (indirectly) provide insights into the quality of cobots that can be a piece of valuable information for the designers. In this sense, identifying and validating a set of key aspects to assess the subjective experience in interaction with robots during collaborative tasks is a stepping stone for benchmarking cobots. We will discuss how, in other domains, researchers developed standardized scales to ensure comparable results regarding the user experience (UX), and to model the differences between systems. Moreover, based on a recent systematic literature review, an initial list of key aspects to evaluate UX with cobots is discussed as a step to build and validate a future tool for unifying how experts evaluate cobots.

How can human researchers use artificial intelligence (AI) to make progress on difficult mechanics problems while retaining control of physical significance, mathematical rigor, and validation? We explore this opportunity through a quantitative stability problem rooted in the Eshelby conjecture. For a uniform dilatational eigenstrain in a homogeneous isotropic solid, we establish a nonlinear two-sided relation between whole-interior strain heterogeneity and a geometry-only distance from the ellipsoid family, with half-order Sobolev scaling that captures morphological length scale. We then develop a complementary finite-shape theory: ellipsoidal subtraction yields an exact residual-field budget from which systematically convergent upper and lower bounds are obtained for a prescribed geometry. Applied to protruded, indented, and necked inclusions, the bounds agree with independent displacement-based finite-element calculations. The study also documents a human-led, AI-assisted research process in which researchers select consequential problems, shape targets, audit arguments, require independent checks, and interpret mechanics, while AI broadens analytical exploration and supports computation. This experience also led us to develop Open Problems in Mechanics, a versioned community-facing map that makes selected mechanics questions, their known/open boundaries, and criteria for progress explicit.
topics: Nonlocal and gradient elasticity in micro/nano structures

documents.abstract: Automated generation of multiple-choice questions (MCQs) represents a viable strategy for scalable assessment and instructional support, but current systems exhibit persistent limitations in distractor quality, reasoning validity, and deployment accessibility. Building on our earlier short paper, YMCQ: Reasoning-Enhanced MCQ Generation, this journal article extends that work by providing a more detailed presentation and explanation of the MCQ generation and multi-stage filtering method introduced there. The method integrates reasoning-based answer generation with misconception-aware distractors, using open-source LLMs fine-tuned on publicly available corpora augmented with synthetic explanations for correct answers and distractors. These augmentations enable the generation of MCQs that are structurally valid, semantically coherent, and pedagogically aligned. The extended presentation further details the method and its implementation in QuizTools, a publicly available platform that supports automated MCQ generation from source materials and enables human-in-the-loop refinement. The pairwise performance evaluation of the generated questions was reported in the short paper; this journal article additionally includes an individual-question quality evaluation, analysis of user edits, and a usability study of QuizTools. The models, datasets, and source code, including over 300,000 quiz items with annotated explanations, are publicly available to facilitate reproducibility and further research in educational NLP.

The increasing availability of legal information in digital form has created a need for intelligent systems that can provide reliable and understandable access to legal documents. Conventional language models may generate fluent responses but can produce unsupported information, particularly when answering complex legal questions or working with multilingual legal content. This paper proposes a Retrieval Augmented Generation based Legal Document Assistant designed to provide grounded responses with verifiable citations. The proposed framework combines multilingual query processing, semantic and lexical document retrieval, relevance based reranking, context aware answer generation, and citation verification within a unified architecture. User queries are first processed according to their language and transformed into representations suitable for multilingual retrieval. Relevant sections from a collection of legal documents are then retrieved and supplied to the language model as supporting context. Each generated response is associated with source references that allow users to trace the information back to the relevant legal document and section. A citation verification mechanism is introduced to identify unsupported statements and improve the reliability of generated answers. The proposed approach is evaluated using retrieval effectiveness, answer relevance, citation correctness, citation coverage, and groundedness across multiple languages. The framework aims to improve accessibility to legal information while reducing unsupported generation and making AI generated legal responses more transparent and traceable. The proposed architecture can serve as a foundation for multilingual legal information systems where accuracy, source verification, and responsible use of artificial intelligence are essential

Background/Objectives: To assess the agreement between an artificial intelligence (AI)-based decision support system (DS System), applied in real time directly on the ultrasound console, and an expert panel for ACR TI-RADS classification of thyroid nodules (TNs) in a region with a history of iodine deficiency and a consequently high prevalence of TNs. Methods: A single-center prospective study including 118 consecutive patients (with 276 TNs) referred for thyroid ultrasound between March and May 2024. DS System ultrasound features, ACR TI-RADS classifications (TR1–TR5) and management recommendations were recorded per TN, with and without the ‘AI-Adapter’ (AI-based modification of the TI-RADS score), and compared to the consensus assessment of a TI-RADS expert panel (paired tests of marginal homogeneity, Cohen’s unweighted and weighted κ; all analyses adjusted for clustering of TNs within patients). Results: No malignancy was identified during 24-month follow-up (composite reference standard; cytology or histology in six TNs). The DS System could be applied to all TNs without technical failure. Marginal distributions differed between the expert panel and the DS System for all ultrasound feature categories except echogenicity (p = 0.23). Interrater agreement ranged from poor (“lobulated or irregular”, κ = −0.08) to substantial (“cystic or almost completely cystic”, κ = 0.62), most frequently slight to fair. TI-RADS classifications showed slight agreement with (κ = 0.04; linear-weighted κ = 0.14) and without AI-Adapter (κ = 0.13; linear-weighted κ = 0.21). The AI-Adapter changed the ACR TI-RADS score by −1.01 ± 1.04 points. Management recommendations showed fair agreement with (κ = 0.23) and without the AI-Adapter (κ = 0.39). Although the number of TR5 ratings was similar (expert panel: 27; DS System: 26 without and 30 with the AI-Adapter), only seven and eight of the 27 TR5 TNs of the expert panel, respectively, were also rated TR5 by the DS System. Conclusions: Real-time application of the DS System on the ultrasound console was technically feasible, but agreement with an expert panel was low. As all TNs were benign, diagnostic accuracy and clinical safety could not be assessed. Validation in cohorts including malignant TNs is required before the DS System can be considered a substitute for expert assessment in regions with a high prevalence of TNs.

documents.abstract: SQUIRL OS RESEARCH DISCLOSURE - READ FIRST: This work is part of an open-book, AI-assisted research program produced under bifurcated governance (a probabilistic AI agent drafts; a deterministic human key approves; a boundary-layer audit checks claims against receipt archives). documents.abstract: Subjective usability scales, such as the SUS and SEQ, are assumed to provide global assessments of user experience. However, emerging evidence suggests that the final interaction has a disproportionate impact on these subjective ratings, potentially leading to inaccurate global usability scores. This study investigated whether establishing a stable expectation of quality through multiple interactions could buffer against such recency effects. Participants completed a series of search tasks in which the quality of the initial and final interactions was systematically varied. Results revealed that the quality of the final interactions dominated the evaluation, regardless of the user’s initial experiences with the website. For instance, even after several positive interactions, final negative interactions reduced usability ratings to levels indistinguishable from those of an entirely bad design. These findings reveal a strong biasing effect that could inadvertently trigger critical redesign decisions based on transient end-of-session frustrations rather than on objective system quality.

Analytical chemistry plays an essential role in the identification, separation, quantification, and characterization of pharmaceutical substances. Recent technological developments have introduced advanced analytical approaches with improved sensitivity, accuracy, selectivity, speed, and reliability.[1] This review focuses on recent research in chromatography, mass spectrometry, spectroscopy, biosensors, Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning (AI/ML), and Green Analytical Chemistry. Modern chromatographic and mass spectrometric techniques enable efficient separation, structural characterization, impurity profiling, and sensitive analysis of complex samples. Spectroscopic techniques provide rapid and non-destructive characterization, while biosensors offer sensitive, rapid, and potentially portable detection systems. AI/ML approaches are increasingly applied for analytical data processing, prediction, pattern recognition, and method optimization. Green analytical approaches aim to minimize hazardous solvents, waste generation, energy consumption, and sample requirements while maintaining analytical performance.[2] The review compares the methodologies, major findings, strengths, limitations, and research gaps reported in recent studies. Overall, the integration of advanced instrumentation, intelligent data analysis, biosensing technologies, and sustainable analytical practices is expected to contribute to the development of faster, more sensitive, reliable, automated, and environmentally sustainable pharmaceutical analytical methods.[1,2].

Neuropsychology is on the anvil of revolution as the digital era has launched a paradigm shift, changing from a data-poor, fragmented discipline to a data-rich, integrated science, enabling more effective translation of research from bench to bedside. Scope of neuropsychology in both investigation and therapeutics is steadily broadening as there have been paradigmatic shifts in brain mapping techniques, advent of non-invasive neuromodulation techniques, and continued technical revolutions, including virtual reality (VR) environments, integration of Large Language Models (LLMs) like GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 and digital cognitive biomarkers, enabling researchers to examine the origins of impairment and enhance diagnostic precision. Certain proactive measures should encompass securing informed consent, whereby participants comprehend the advantages and risks of involvement, addressing social and cultural disparities in neuroethics, and reconciling individual rights with collective benefits to optimise progress while preserving the rights and dignity of individuals. The future of neuropsychology will rely on utilising technological advances to enhance scientific comprehension of brain-behaviour relationships and to guarantee that advancements result in inclusive, culturally attuned, and patient-centred therapy.

Existing research on interorganizational network dynamics has largely treated network change as gradual, local, and primarily oriented toward private organizational advantage. Yet contemporary cooperative interorganizational systems are highly interconnected across industrial sectors and geographies and are routinely exposed to shocks that simultaneously disable multiple organizations or relationships among them. These shocks stem from pandemics, natural disasters, wars, sanctions, and cascading partner failures, and can rapidly reconfigure whole‑network architectures and undermine collective outcomes. In light of this new reality, we reconceptualize interorganizational networks as loci of frequent, punctuated change at the whole network level, with primary implications for collective outcomes. We develop this reconceptualization through a robustness–resilience lens, defining network robustness as an interorganizational network’s capacity to maintain its collective outcomes in the immediate aftermath of a shock, and network resilience as its capacity to recover and potentially surpass pre‑shock collective outcomes over the longer term. We then outline the theoretical and methodological opportunities that this robustness–resilience perspective opens for the study of network change.

documents.abstract: The guarantee of a good and healthy environment is a constitutional right of citizens as mandated by Article 28H paragraph (1) of the 1945 Constitution of the Republic of Indonesia and Law Number 18 of 2008 concerning Waste Management. This study aims to analyze the operational conditions and environmental dynamics at Parit Enam Final Disposal Site in Pangkalpinang C ity, evaluate the harmonization of technical regulations concerning compensation for negative impacts, and formulate a concept for reconstructing compensation rights based on sustainable governance synergy. The research method employed is empirical legal research (socio-legal research) using a sociological-juridical approach, combining field studies through in-depth interviews and observation with library research. The results show that, with accumulated waste reaching 184,992 m³/year, technical control efforts by the Environmental Agency have been implemented; however, the implementation of compensation for communities in the buffer zone still requires stronger technical legal foundations at the local level so that it can be implemented in a more structured and transparent manner. This study recommends reconstructing compensation rights by transforming them from a passive scheme into a participatory empowerment scheme based on three main pillars: occupational health and safety, environmental infrastructure improvement, and community circular-economic empowerment through the integration of organic waste processing. Collaborative synergy among local government, communities, and the private sector is key to realizing environmental justice and sustainable urban governance.

The advent of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in postgraduate research and education is rapidly unsettling traditional student-supervisor relationships, thereby reshaping the role of supervisors. While AI-powered tools such as Grammarly, QuillBot, and Thesify assist postgraduate students in idea generation and mapping, searching, reviewing and analysing complex data, and improving academic tone, they also highlight significant challenges, including the erosion of critical thinking and independence, as well as issues of accuracy and ethical dilemmas in higher education. Grounded in Foucault's (1979) power-knowledge dynamics, this chapter provides an analytical framework for understanding how AI restructures mentor-mentee dynamics, establishing a different set of circumstances—a shift from a mentor-novice framework to a hybrid model. Moreover, this work contributes to ongoing debates regarding the implications for supervisory roles and mentorship models for supervisors and students in higher education in the age of AI.

The rapid growth of Generative Artificial Intelligence in higher education has made assessment more complex. Its importance lies in protecting genuine learning and academic integrity in AI rich environments. The main objective of this chapter is to explain how assessment and feedback practices can be redesigned to measure real understanding instead of automated output. The chapter shows that authentic tasks, staged submissions, reflection, and oral interaction improve validity and fairness. Key findings suggest that formative feedback, clear AI guidelines, and process based evaluation strengthen integrity. The chapter concludes that thoughtful redesign helps institutions maintain standards while adapting to technological change.

Low-resolution tactile interfaces often require users to identify spatial codes through active sequential exploration, but the interaction costs and error structures of reference-assisted sparse-code decoding remain undercharacterized. We studied how 15 novice users decoded Braille-like alphabetic patterns on a 3 × 2 vibrotactile interface using blindfolded tactile exploration followed by visual reference-chart consultation. Participants completed a baseline single-location discrimination task and a three-block character-decoding task without explicit letter-pattern training or trial-wise correctness feedback. Single-location performance was near ceiling, whereas character-decoding accuracy increased across blocks. Exploration accounted for the larger share of task time, but incorrect trials showed a disproportionate prolongation of the composite post-exploration reference-assisted stage. Errors were structured by pattern similarity: most occurred between patterns separated by a Hamming distance of 1, and higher dot counts were associated with lower accuracy and longer response times. These findings inform low-resolution vibrotactile interface design by characterizing interaction costs and pattern confusability.

This article presents a comprehensive transdisciplinary review of the ways in which artificial intelligence(AI) and immersive technologies are transforming foundational concepts of authorship, ethics, and creativitywithin contemporary architecture and spatial design. The traditional notion of the architect as a singular,authoritative creator increasingly is challenged by computational processes that introduce generative, autonomous,and distributed forms of design agency. Through a synthesis of architectural theory, AI ethics, media studies,and posthuman philosophy, the review interrogates the shifting locus of authorship in design environmentsmediated by intelligent systems and extended reality (XR) platforms. At the core of this inquiry is an ontological reframing of authorship, informed by scholars such as RosiBraidotti, Tony Fry, Humberto Maturana, and Anne-Marie Willis. These frameworks position the architect notas an originator of form, but as a participant in a relational field of human and non-human agents, includingalgorithms, data, environments, and users. Adopting an ontological design lens, under which design practicesand their tools co‑produce forms of life and ways of world‑making, the article argues that AI/XR systems donot merely assist representation but actively configure professional authorship, agency, and ethics. This framinglinks practical workflows to normative guidance for disclosure, responsibility, and education. The review exploreshow generative design, neural networks, and parametric modeling redefine design intention and originality,situating authorship as a curatorial and computationally entangled process. In parallel, immersive media suchas virtual and augmented reality introduce new forms of user co-authorship and spatial manipulation, promptingethical questions about consent, agency, presence, and the authenticity of digital space. The article maps emerging discourses around design accountability, legal attribution, algorithmic bias, anddata governance, proposing an expanded ethical vocabulary for posthuman design practices. Through a criticalexamination of scholarly literature, experimental studios, and case-based applications, the review identifiesepistemological and practical challenges in reconciling human-centered traditions with distributed technologicalagency. Ultimately, this article argues for a redefinition of authorship as a dynamic, ethically situated, andontologically pluralistic concept in architecture. It advocates for the development of integrative frameworksthat embed ethical foresight and philosophical reflexivity into AI-augmented and immersive design methodologies.By repositioning the architect as a negotiator within hybrid systems of creativity and control, the articlecontributes a forward-looking perspective to architectural theory, technological practice, and planning discourse.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly changing how assessment is designed and conducted in higher education. While AI tools can improve feedback, efficiency, and personalization, they also raise serious concerns related to academic integrity, fairness, transparency, privacy, and trust. This chapter critically examines AI-powered assessment as not just a technical process, but a socio-pedagogical and ethical practice. It highlights the limitations of surveillance-based and detection-focused approaches and argues for a shift toward authentic, integrity-driven assessment. Special attention is given to Global South and resource-constrained contexts, where issues of access, bias, and inequality are more pronounced. The chapter proposes guiding principles for responsible AI use that prioritize learning, equity, student agency, and human judgment in higher education assessment.

documents.abstract: As artificial intelligence (AI) tools and digital platforms become embedded in everyday communication, governments face growing pressure to regulate misinformation, hate speech, and other harmful online content while protecting freedom of expression. This study examines regulatory debates in Mongolia’s digital information space and argues that regulatory acceptance and legitimacy cannot be explained through an individual-centered perspective alone. It first organizes Mongolia’s digital governance challenges through four interrelated forms of uncertainty: cultural, ethical, institutional, and relational. This approach highlights Mongolia’s hybrid cultural environment, where collectivist traditions intersect with expanding individualism, and where public judgments about regulation are shaped by relationships and trust. Drawing on a quota-sampling survey of two hundred and seventy respondents from urban and rural Mongolia, the study employs Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) and multi-group analysis to examine the direct, mediating, and moderating effects of four trust dimensions: strong-tie trust, weak-tie trust, institutional trust, and platform trust. The findings show that institutional trust is the strongest positive predictor of regulatory acceptance, followed by platform trust, strong-tie trust, and weak-tie trust. Relational trust statistically mediates the relationship between freedom-of-expression concerns and regulatory acceptance, suggesting that concerns about censorship are interpreted through broader trust environments. Urban-rural and generational differences further condition the effects of trust. The Mongolian case illustrates broader challenges faced by small democracies and platform-dependent societies, where domestic regulatory capacity remains limited while global platforms shape the public sphere. The study demonstrates the need to understand regulatory legitimacy through relationships, trust, and cultural context, not solely legal systems or individual literacy alone.

Long-term personalized tutoring requires language models to translate a learner's evolving history into appropriate instructional support. Existing LLM-based tutoring systems use memory and retrieval to personalize responses, but the pedagogical rationale linking historical evidence to teaching strategies is not always explicit. We introduce RegulaTutor, a theory-informed framework for long-term personalized tutoring that connects historical evidence, learner interpretation, and learner-facing instruction. Guided by self-regulated learning (SRL) research, its tutoring harness operationalizes a cognitive, affective, metacognitive, and motivational (CAMM) framework for deriving evidence-supported learner interpretations and teaching policies. The resulting policies retain links to their supporting evidence and are updated as new observations arrive. This staged workflow also supports systematic refinement through PairRoute, an offline procedure that uses intermediate execution records to distinguish harness, model, and mixed failures. PairRoute proposes and evaluates targeted harness revisions, then constructs reviewed stage-level supervision for confirmed model failures remaining under the selected harness. We focus this refinement on historical evidence acquisition, which underpins personalized instruction and allows outputs to be checked against learning records and reference answers. RegulaTutor improves historical-evidence accuracy, learner diagnosis, and judged teaching quality on average across evaluated model configurations. PairRoute results show an endpoint improvement in standalone-model historical-evidence accuracy over the refinement trajectory. Together, these results highlight RegulaTutor's potential to support lifelong personalized education through instructional policies that evolve with learner histories and targeted improvements to the tutoring system.

documents.abstract: How users come to perceive an AI not merely as capable but as intentionally oriented toward them in a specific relational capacity remains undertheorized. We propose relational role attribution (RRA) as a discrete psychological construct addressing this gap, positioned as a precursor to downstream relational outcomes rather than a reframing of trust. A PRISMA-ScR scoping review charted 1223 reports at full text against a registered protocol, including 466. Of 179 records excluded for establishing no relational or social role for the agent, 122 (68.2%) nonetheless manipulated or measured anthropomorphism: the field reaches the cue and stops short of the attribution. RRA comprises two concurrent components, a relational inference of social orientation and a role assignment drawn from contextual and communicative cues, checked against the expectancy the user brings. Naming the attribution allows findings accumulated separately across marketing, teaming, and communication literatures to constrain one another, and scaffolds role-specific design principles.
